Match: Chapter one. Six companies, no names.

Start with a game. Here are six real American companies, with their names taken off. For each, five numbers from its latest accounts. How many cents of operating profit it keeps from each dollar of sales. How many dollars of sales it makes from each dollar of things it owns. How many dollars of things it owns for each dollar its owners put in: the rest is borrowed. And how much of each dollar of sales goes back into research, and into new buildings and equipment. The six are a warehouse grocer, Costco; a software company, Microsoft; a bank, JPMorgan Chase; a power company, NextEra Energy; an airline, Delta; and a drug maker, Eli Lilly. Match them. One clue: company B turns over its assets more than three times a year, and company D owns twelve dollars of things for every dollar of its own. Keep your answers; they are revealed near the end of this part, by which time you will be able to say why.
Ledger: Let's keep the books of a small business ourselves. A woman opens a bakery. On the left, everything the bakery has. On the right, where the money for it came from: borrowed, owed, or put in by the owner. Pacioli's rule is that every entry changes the two sides by the same amount, or moves money within one side, so the totals always match.
The owner puts in her savings, forty thousand dollars. The bakery now has forty thousand of cash, and that cash came from her.
The bank lends twenty thousand. More cash, and a debt to the bank on the other side.
She buys an oven for forty-five thousand. Cash goes down, an oven goes up. Nothing new came in from anyone, so the right-hand side does not move.
The miller delivers three thousand dollars of flour, to be paid in thirty days. Flour on one side, a debt to the miller on the other.
She bakes, and sells six thousand dollars of bread for cash...
...and three thousand to a cafe that will pay next month. Where did that nine thousand come from? From her customers, and it belongs to her: profit, on the owner's side.
But the bread used the flour, three thousand dollars of it. The flour is gone, and the profit is three thousand smaller.
And she pays her baker four thousand in wages. Cash down, profit down.

Eight entries, and the two sides still agree: 65,000 dollars of things on the left, and 65,000 dollars of claims on them on the right. The left side is the bakery's assets. The right side is its liabilities, what it owes, and its equity, what belongs to the owner, including the 2,000 dollars of profit so far. That balance is not luck. It is how the system is built, and it is why a company's balance sheet always balances.
Income: Now a whole year. The bakery sells sixty thousand loaves and cakes at three dollars sixty: 216,000 dollars of sales. Take off what went into them, the flour, butter and fillings, and 138,000 dollars is left: the gross profit, 64 percent of sales. Then the costs of being open at all: the staff, the owner's own pay and the rent, a hundred and fifteen thousand. And one cost that is never paid in the year at all. The oven cost forty-five thousand and should last ten years, so each year carries a tenth of it, four thousand five hundred dollars. Accountants call it depreciation. What is left is the operating profit, 18,500 dollars: what the business itself earns. Interest to the bank and tax to the government come off, and the net profit, the bottom line, is 13,509 dollars: about six cents on each dollar of sales.

The income statement of a real company has the same shape, and the shape is the business. Here is one dollar of sales at five companies. Costco: 87 cents pays for the goods on its shelves, nine for the warehouses, staff and overheads, and less than four cents is left as operating profit. Microsoft: the copies of its software cost almost nothing, so most of its costs are people and data centres, and it keeps 47 cents. Delta: 28 cents to its people, 15 for fuel, 48 for everything else an airline needs, from aircraft to airports, and nine cents of profit. Eli Lilly: 17 cents to make its medicines, 20 on research for the next ones, 17 to sell them, and 40 cents of profit. NextEra, the power company: its largest cost is depreciation, the wear on its power plants and wires, 24 cents of every dollar, a cost that, like the bakery's oven, was paid for years ago. A bank's statement looks different again: of JPMorgan's dollar, 52 cents goes on its people and offices and about 8 on loans expected to go bad.
Balance: At the end of the year the accountant draws the two sides of the book as a picture of the business on one day: the balance sheet. On the left, what the bakery has: 25,447 dollars of cash; 11,836 dollars that cafes owe it, because they pay twenty days after delivery; a little flour; and the oven, now worth less after a year's wear. On the right, who paid for it all: the miller, who has not been paid yet; the bank; and the owner, whose forty thousand is now 53,509 dollars, because the year's profit of 13,509 dollars was kept in the business. Every company's balance sheet is this picture, and the right-hand side is the interesting one: whose money is the business running on?

Now five real ones, each drawn the same height. JPMorgan Chase, a bank: of 4.4 trillion dollars of assets, a third is loans to its customers. And on the right, almost six dollars in ten are deposits: the bank's biggest supplier of money is the people who keep their savings there. Its owners' money is eight cents in the dollar. Everything else is borrowed. NextEra: almost three quarters of what it has is power plants, turbines, solar farms and wires, paid for largely with long-term debt. Costco: a fifth of what it has is the stock on its shelves, and the money it owes its suppliers is larger than that stock. Its suppliers are paying for the shelves. Delta: a fifth of its balance sheet is money from customers for tickets not yet flown and SkyMiles not yet spent, more than 16 billion dollars, held before a seat is used. And Microsoft: mostly its owners' money, and its biggest single asset now is data centres. Who funds a business, and in what form, tells you a great deal about the business.
Cash: Chapter five. Profit is not cash.

The bakery made 13,509 dollars of profit. How much cash did it make? Start from the profit. Add back the oven's wear: it was a cost, but no money left the till for it this year. Take off the 11,836 dollars the cafes still owe: sales counted, cash not received. Take off the flour sitting in the store room. Add the miller's bill, not yet paid. The business itself brought in 10,447 dollars of cash, less than its profit. And the oven cost forty-five thousand in cash this year, so over the year the bakery's own operations used up 34,553 dollars more than they produced. The owner's savings and the bank paid for the difference. That is why accounts come with a third statement, the cash-flow statement: profit is an opinion about the year, cash is a fact.

Now let the bakery grow. It opens a new shop and buys a new oven every year, sales rise sixty percent a year, and to win the cafes it gives them sixty days to pay instead of twenty. Its profit rises every year, from 13,509 dollars to 79,319 dollars. And its cash runs out in the second year. Every extra sale ties up more money in what the cafes owe and in stock, and every new shop needs an oven paid for up front. Many small businesses fail this way: profitable on paper and out of cash. The cure is not more profit; it is more patient money, from the owner, the bank or investors, or slower growth.

Giant companies face the same arithmetic. Microsoft, in the year to June 2026, reported 133.7 billion dollars of net income, and its operations brought in 182.9 billion dollars of cash, more than its profit, because the wear on its equipment is a cost that does not drain cash, and customers pay for subscriptions in advance. But it spent 115.9 billion dollars on data centres, chips and buildings for artificial intelligence, almost twice as much as a year before. What was left, the free cash, was 67 billion dollars, half its profit. And in the first quarter of the next year, free cash fell again, as spending kept rising. NextEra, the power company, spends far more than its operations bring in, every year: 24.1 billion dollars on new plants and wires in 2025 against 12.5 billion dollars of operating cash. The difference is borrowed, and repaid over decades from the bills of customers who have little choice of supplier. A utility is built to be cash-hungry; a software company is not, and for the AI build-out, Microsoft has chosen to become a little more like a utility.
Intermission: An intermission. For most of its history Microsoft was the model of a business that needs almost no capital: in fiscal 2010 it spent 2 billion dollars on buildings and equipment. Then came the cloud, and the spending grew year after year. And then artificial intelligence: 115.9 billion dollars in fiscal 2026, about sixty times as much, and the company has said it will spend more in the year after. The gold line is the cash its business brings in. The gap between them has closed fast.

The story so far. Every transaction is written twice, so the balance sheet always balances. The income statement says how much of each dollar of sales a company keeps. The balance sheet says what it owns, and whose money paid for it. And the cash-flow statement says whether the profit turned into money. Next: how speed, margin and borrowing combine, and whether a business earns its keep.
Costco: Chapter six. Paid before it pays.

Costco keeps less than four cents of each dollar of sales. Yet it earned 9.2 billion dollars in its last fiscal year. Two things explain it, and both are in the accounts. The first is time. A pallet of goods arrives at a Costco warehouse. On average it is sold within about 27 days, and members pay at the till, on the spot. Costco pays its supplier after about 31 days. So Costco has been paid before it pays. Across the whole company, the money it owes suppliers, 22.6 billion dollars, is larger than all the stock on its shelves. Its suppliers, in effect, finance its shelves, and the faster it grows, the more of their money it holds. The bakery that gave cafes sixty days ran out of cash; Costco gets the opposite deal.

The second thing is the membership card. Costco had 84.1 million paid members at the end of its 2026 fiscal year, and each one spent about 3,672 dollars there in the year. On those purchases Costco made about 70 dollars of operating profit. And each member also paid about 72 dollars for the card itself. Membership fees were 5.9 billion dollars, 51 percent of Costco's operating income. Costco sells the goods with less than two cents of operating profit on each dollar, and earns half its profit selling the right to shop there. The low prices keep the members renewing, and the renewals pay for the low prices.
DuPont: Chapter seven. Margin, speed and borrowing.

Donaldson Brown's split, extended by one more step, is the most useful formula in this part. What the owners care about is the return on their money: the year's profit for every dollar they have in the business. It is the product of three things. The margin: how much profit each dollar of sales leaves. The speed: how many dollars of sales each dollar of assets produces in a year. And the borrowing: how many dollars of assets each dollar of the owners' money supports, the rest coming from lenders and suppliers. For the bakery: a margin of 6.3 percent, times 2.7 dollars of sales per dollar of assets, times 1.5, gives 25 percent on the owner's money. There are three ways to a good return, and each industry takes a different one.

Put the six companies on a map of the first two. Across, the speed: dollars of sales per dollar of assets. Up, the margin. The dashed curves join points with the same return on assets, margin times speed. Costco is far to the right: it sells 3.4 dollars of goods a year for every dollar it owns, at a margin of 3 cents. Microsoft is far up: 40 cents of profit on each dollar, but only 44 cents of sales a year from each dollar of data centres and everything else. Opposite businesses; both earn ten percent or more on their assets. Lilly is high and fairly fast. The airline is in the middle. The power company and the bank sit low and slow: NextEra needs a dollar of assets for every thirteen cents of yearly sales, and JPMorgan earns 1.3 cents a year on each dollar of assets.

Now the third lever. Multiply the return on assets by how far the owners' money is stretched, and you get the return on the owners' money. The bank earns only 1.3 percent on its assets, but it holds 12 dollars of assets for every dollar of its owners' money, so its owners earn about 16 percent. Borrowing is the bank's business. It cuts both ways. With eight cents of owners' money behind each dollar of assets, a loss of eight cents in the dollar on what it has lent and invested would wipe the owners out. That is why regulators watch banks' capital so closely. And at the top, Lilly's 78 percent is partly the drug business and partly arithmetic: years of buying back its own shares shrank the owners' money on the balance sheet, so every dollar of profit is divided by less. A high return on equity can mean a great business, or a lot of borrowing, or both. The formula tells you which.
Roic: Chapter eight. The return on capital.

Profit is not the same as a good business, because the owners' money is not free. They could have put it somewhere else. Suppose that elsewhere, at the same risk, they could expect eight percent a year. That is the business's cost of capital. Now they put a hundred dollars into it. If it earns twelve dollars a year, a return on capital of twelve percent, investors will pay about a hundred and fifty dollars for that stream: twelve divided by eight percent. Value was created. If it earns six dollars, it is profitable, and worth only seventy-five. Every dollar put in became seventy-five cents. And a company like that destroys more value the faster it grows, because every new dollar it invests shrinks too. Growth only helps when the return on capital is above its cost.

Here is the return on capital for five of our six companies, measured one simple way: operating profit after a standard tax, divided by the owners' money plus long-term debt. Lilly, Microsoft and Costco earn between 22 and 31 percent: far above any reasonable cost of capital. Each has something competitors cannot easily copy: patents on a medicine, software everyone already uses, members who renew. Delta earned about thirteen percent in 2025; an airline's return swings with fuel and the economy, as Part six, on the cycle, will show. NextEra shows about 5 percent, and the measure is unkind to it: a regulated utility is allowed a return close to its cost of capital, and much of NextEra's profit arrives as clean-energy tax credits, which are booked as lower income tax, below the operating line this measure uses. And the last bar is Enron in 2000, by Fortune's estimate: about seven percent, the return of a Treasury bond, for a company priced as a star. That number comes back at the end of this part.
Units: Chapter nine. One seat, one member.

Accounts become vivid when you divide them by the unit the business sells. For an airline, the unit is one seat flown one mile. In 2025 Delta took in 21.26 cents of revenue for every seat it flew a mile, full or empty, and spent 19.31 cents. Take one seat from New York to Los Angeles, about two thousand five hundred miles. It brings in about 526 dollars. About 145 dollars of that pays Delta's people, 82 dollars the fuel, and 251 dollars the aircraft, airports, maintenance and everything else. What is left is about 48 dollars. And the arithmetic rebuilds the accounts: a margin of 1.95 cents, times the 298 billion seat miles Delta flew, is 5.8 billion dollars, which is Delta's operating income for the year.

Now one more line from Delta's accounts. Every time someone pays with a Delta SkyMiles card, American Express buys miles from Delta to give its cardholders, with marketing and other benefits in the same contract. In 2025 those payments came to 8.2 billion dollars, up eleven percent, and Delta expects ten billion within a few years. Spread over every seat it flew, that is about 68 dollars on our seat to Los Angeles, more than the 48 dollars the airline kept from it after all its costs. Delta's accounts describe an airline; they also describe a loyalty business attached to one, which sells miles to a bank. That is unit economics: divide by the right unit, and the business underneath shows through.
Segments: A company's totals can hide several different businesses, and the notes break them out as segments. Microsoft reports three. Productivity and Business Processes: Office, LinkedIn and Dynamics. 140 billion dollars of revenue in fiscal 2026, and an operating margin of 60 percent: subscriptions to software hundreds of millions of people already use. Intelligent Cloud: Azure and the server business, 137.8 billion dollars, up thirty percent, with Azure itself up 41 percent. Its margin is lower, 41 percent, and its costs rose 44 percent, which Microsoft says was driven by its investment in AI infrastructure: the data centres of the last chapters show up here. More Personal Computing: Windows, Surface, Xbox and search advertising, 54.1 billion dollars, slightly smaller than a year before, at 27 percent. So the profit is in Office, the growth is in the cloud, and the spending is for the cloud's future. One set of totals; three businesses with different economics.

Segments can also be products. Of Eli Lilly's 65 billion dollars of revenue in 2025, 56 percent came from two names, Mounjaro and Zepbound, which are the same medicine, tirzepatide, sold for diabetes and for weight loss. That one molecule explains most of Lilly's growth, its margin and its return on capital. It also tells you the risk: the accounts of a drug maker are as strong as its patents, and every patent expires.
Mislead: Chapter eleven. Where the accounts mislead.

Accounts are rules, and rules leave gaps. Six to watch for, each from this part's companies. Research. Lilly spent 13.3 billion dollars in 2025 on finding the next medicines. The rules count all of it as a cost in the year it is spent, so the most valuable things Lilly owns, its future drugs, appear nowhere on its balance sheet. Pay in shares. Microsoft gave its employees 12.4 billion dollars of stock in fiscal 2026. It is a cost in the income statement but no cash leaves, so it is added back in the cash-flow statement; the owners pay instead, as their share of the company is diluted. Gains on paper. Microsoft's net income included 6.5 billion dollars of net gains from its investment in OpenAI, mostly because OpenAI reorganized and raised money from others. Real, perhaps, but not cash, and not from selling software. Goodwill: 119.7 billion dollars on Microsoft's balance sheet, the premium it paid for companies like LinkedIn and Activision Blizzard over the value of their own assets. It cannot be sold on its own, and if an acquisition disappoints, it is written down. The company's own measures. Delta reports its cost per seat mile, 19.31 cents, and also an adjusted one that leaves out fuel and some other items, 13.86 cents. Both are useful; only one is the cost. Always find the reconciliation. And estimates. JPMorgan booked 14.2 billion dollars for loans it expects to go bad. That is a forecast, and a bank that is too hopeful will look more profitable than it is, until the loans fail.
Reveal: Back to the six companies with no names. Company B, turning over its assets three times a year on a margin of under four cents, is Costco. Company D, with twelve dollars of assets on every dollar of its owners' money, is the bank, JPMorgan. Company A, spending 88 cents of every dollar of sales on new equipment and turning over its assets only once every eight years, is the power company, NextEra. Company C, putting twenty cents of each dollar into research, is Eli Lilly. Company F, with the fattest margin and thirty-five cents of every dollar now going into data centres, is Microsoft. And company E, thin margin, heavy equipment and plenty of borrowing, is Delta. If you got most of them, you can already read the shape of a business from its accounts. If you did not, look again at the two numbers that gave most of them away: the speed and the borrowing.
Called: Every part ends with a forecast. This one was made by a journalist. In March 2001, Enron, the Houston energy trader, was a stock-market favourite: its revenue had just more than doubled, to over a hundred billion dollars, and its shares had returned 89 percent the year before. Bethany McLean of Fortune asked a simple question: how exactly does Enron make its money? She had read the accounts. The shares were priced at about fifty-five times the last year's earnings, yet the return on the capital in the business was around seven percent, about what a Treasury bond paid. And the cash did not match the profit. Cash from operations had fallen from 1.6 billion dollars in 1998 to 1.2 billion in 1999, and to just 100 million in the first nine months of 2000, while reported earnings kept rising. Enron said she did not understand the business.

Here are the accounts she was reading, as Enron filed them for 2000, a few weeks after her article. Revenue more than doubled, to over a hundred billion dollars, almost all of it from its wholesale energy business. Net income crept up, to just under a billion. And cash from operations, after the weak first nine months, leapt to 4.8 billion dollars for the full year. A Senate investigation later found how: deals the banks called prepays, loans dressed up as energy trades so that borrowed money arrived as operating cash, about eight billion dollars of them over six years. In November 2001 Enron restated four years of profits, cutting them by 591 million dollars, and on the second of December it filed for bankruptcy. The accounts did not tell the whole truth. But the gap between profit and cash, and a return on capital that never matched the story, were there for a careful reader.

And this series' own call, logged today. In its fiscal year to June 2027, Microsoft's free cash flow, the cash from its operations less what it spends on equipment, will be lower than the 67 billion dollars of fiscal 2026, even though its operating profit will be higher. The reasoning: in the first quarter, spending on equipment doubled, and free cash fell to 18.6 billion dollars from 25.7 billion dollars; and the company has guided to spending of about 170 billion dollars in the year, including leases. What would make us wrong: a slowdown in the building, or cash from customers arriving faster than expected. We put it at sixty-five percent, and we will score it on the annual report next summer.
